Early each week, we bring you a conversation from our episode of The New Yorker Radio Hour.
The New Yorker Radio Hour is a co-production of WNYC and The New Yorker.
Welcome to The New Yorker Radio Hour. I'm David Remnick.
Conventional wisdom in politics, well, it can turn on a dime, as we've just seen.
Weeks ago on this program, we were raising serious questions about whether free and fair midterm elections would even take place.
take place. Now, call it a tsunami, call it an earthquake, what have you, the Democrats
will hold large majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Maybe most shocking of all, the president skipped right over denial and immediately
began finger pointing at his allies, something and someone to blame for the defeat.
Our guest today, Pete Buttigieg, is no stranger to quick turns in politics. In a few months
of 2019, he went from running a small Indiana city, South Bend, to emerging as a plausible
candidate for the presidency. And while he came up short, his star did not dim. He joined
the Biden administration, and this year he's been one of the most in-demand Democratic
surrogates on the campaign trail. Buttigieg is widely expected to be a candidate once
again in 2028.
But two years can be a very long time, as we've seen. If the Democrats are going to
hold on to victory long enough to elect a president, then they'll have to figure out
how to make an impact in these next two years, even with an angry lame duck in the White
House.
I asked Pete Buttigieg what that might look like.
We're speaking now after a momentous election.
Tell me how you're feeling and maybe more deeply, what does this all mean?
Well, it's extraordinary.
And I think it is the beginning of a change in the era that we're living in.
Now a lot depends on what happens next.
This is more of an opening than it is an answer.
But I think fundamentally there was a widespread
and wholesale rejection of Donald Trump's policies
on the congressional Republicans who enabled him.
The American people clearly saw corruption
and their economic frustrations
as two categories of things that were related to each other.
They voted accordingly.
The president invited the electorate
to imagine that he was on the ballot.
I think what happened is we took him up on that.
And that's why there was such just a resounding, extraordinary defeat for the Republicans,
frankly, beyond anything that I really hoped could happen, even though I was working hard
to do my best to help make it happen.
But I think it's fair to say that the Democratic Party's brand as such did not exactly get
soaring ratings.
So is there a possibility that you interpret or that this election can be overinterpreted
as an endorsement of the Democratic Party rather than a repudiation of Donald Trump
and MAGA specifically?
Yeah, that's part of what I mean when I say this is an opening rather than a solution.
What has happened is Democrats have been given a chance.
This doesn't mean everybody suddenly fell in love with the Democratic Party.
What it means is that Democratic candidates sometimes as part of the party, sometimes
in spite of the party label, persuaded voters that we had better answers.
And I do think one thing that's important to recognize is, you know, for years now,
it has been the case that democratic policies have been more popular than the democratic party
or democratic politicians.
And by the way, this is new.
When I came of age, our position on taxing the wealthy, for example, was not as popular as it was now.
Our position on healthcare certainly is much more popular now than it used to be.
A whole bunch of things we used to be on defense around are now things people believe, but
we still weren't winning elections.
So I think the best thing that could happen is for our brand and our politicians to come
in line with our policy commitments, the most important ones that really unite about two-thirds
of the country and pretty much 100% of the party.
If we stick to those in the new congressional majorities and state trifectas that have been
then I think there's an enormous opportunity to change what people assume and what people
picture when they picture the Democratic Party.
Now, this isn't the first time people have declared the Trump era over. I can with some
abashments say that the New Yorker had a headline eight years ago on a piece online.
It said in essence, you know, this is the end of the Trump era or it's about to end.
I forget which flagrant piece of misbehavior it was commenting on.
But I think we can agree that was premature.
Are you ready to declare the fever broken now?
Look, we thought the fever was broken around January 6 and many other times.
This was the Trump era, even when he was out of power.
And right now, he's in power, at least he's in power in the White House.
So I do think it's way too soon to say the era has come to an end.
You felt that acutely while you were in the Biden administration
that you were still living in the Trump era when you look back on it?
In retrospect, you can see it. Yeah, even when we were in charge, it was kind of his world and we
were living in it. I would really say ever since he came down that escalator 10 or 11 years ago,
that's been the case. I think he represented a middle finger to the status quo. And people were
outraged at the way things worked in this country, not always connecting that to particular
policy decisions or individual commitments by one part of the other, but just a desire to change
things that ran so strong that for some, the idea of just kind of burning it all down sounded better
than trying to have their lives improve with the status quo. And this is the thing that Democrats
need to now be paying attention to, because part of what was a trap for us in 2016,
just as it was in 2024, was that in our horror at the destruction of so many institutions of
American life, we became defenders of those institutions in ways that made it feel like
we were defending a status quo that, frankly, we didn't love that much either. Now is a time to
make clear we understand our task is not to go back and find all the bits and the shards of the
status quo that have been smashed to pieces, tape them back up together and give people some
semblance of what we used to have. This is about making sure that we're prepared for what's next
and that we're very selective about which norms, institutions, even agencies we really
do need to put back together and which ones need to be fully replaced now that they've
been destroyed.
So here's something that happened.
J.D. Vance, the vice president of the United States, the vice president for president who
was so clearly repudiated by the American electorate in so many states, issues a statement
on Twitter, not only criticizing the war that the president single-handedly brought us into,
but also clearly or implicitly announcing himself as the candidate and putting a big
distance between himself and the president of the United States.
Are we off to the races?
It feels that way.
Look, we watched a lot of Republican candidates, mainly members of Congress, trying to find
some way to keep the Trump stink from attaching to them.
And in almost every case, they fail.
Now, if you can't keep that stink off of you as a member of the Republican Party who maybe

that administration.
Let's be clear.

And the fact that he deep down knows better, the fact that he originally compared Donald
Trump to Hitler before he got on board doesn't make all of this better.
It makes all of this worse.
And you think he meant Hitler in a bad way?
I have to think he didn't mean it in a good way.
Exactly.
Fox almost as much as Sean Hannity. And when you talk to those guys, do you get a sense from them
that they know what's what?
No. I was toggling the channels, watching how Fox was trying to make sense of this. And

Things like the tariffs and the tax cuts for the rich were

comprehensive, thoroughgoing rejection of Trump and the Republican Party, hopefully
at some point that leads to a little more introspection.
You see it happening online a little bit.
I don't know how long it'll take for that
to catch up to the Fox Newsroom.
Well, is there a chance that the Democratic Party
could overinterpret this election victory
as comprehensive as it is, as stunning as it is?
Yeah, there are many ways
that Democrats could get this wrong.
For example, while pursuing the oversight agenda
is very important, we need accountability,
we need standards in this country.
If for one second it appears that a democratic Congress is more interested in retribution
than putting money in people's pockets and getting them relief from these disastrous
economic policies, that's going to be a real problem, substantively and politically.
Then how do you solve the problem, the moral problem, the moral and political problem of
balancing the urge to impeach, for example, but also the desire to set a moral and political
standard of proper behavior. If you want to fight corruption, all kinds of malfeasance
and offense, how do you do that and at the same time not fall into it being subject number
one, two, and three in Washington?
Well, our North Star is making the American people better off, improving everyday life,
making it all more affordable. An accountability agenda could come at the expense of that,
but a smart accountability agenda would actually be serving that because there's a direct
relationship between bad policy outcomes and potential corruption in the administration.
I'm thinking of everything from the bridge between here in Michigan and Canada that got
delayed evidently because a Trump superback donor got to Howard Lutnik to what happened
to the victims of fraudsters who have been pardoned by President Trump and how all of
that came about.
The ability for companies to get somehow get an exemption to put toxic chemicals in the
air or in the ground or get a pass on dangerous food or drug products.
I mean, the list goes on and on and on.
And there is potentially a relationship between those bad policies that hurt people and the
corruption.
So I think when we're thinking about accountability, the focus isn't on which Trump official or
relative to go after.
The focus is on which victims we can support because there are real victims of this from
ice abuses to victims of corruption.
But what are you telling me? Are you against any impeachment hearings of any kind, whether it's
against the president or Pete Hexeth or...?
Yeah, I'm not very interested in impeachment, especially when it comes to the president. I'm
more interested in things that will illuminate the patterns of corruption, that will empower the
victims of abuses by this administration, and that will establish there certain kind of behaviors.
I would focus on the behaviors, not the people. I mean, the people will be held accountable,
but it's about behaviors that would be wrong whether they were done by a Democrat, an independent,
or a Republican. Because the other thing about this accountability agenda is if we get it right,
just like the popular economic policies, I believe, and they are a call back to things that most
Americans can agree on. If we get it wrong, this could be divisive. If we get this right,
it is unifying because part of what success looks like for the country is to get to a place where
Even people who supported this, even people who are part of it, are able to step back and be as

And my experience in the past has been that the candidates who are the most competitive,

It's not as simple as that.
It's different from that.
And I think that, you know, one thing that we're seeing,

is that the candidates who did the best
are not all the ones who have been considered,
quote unquote, low risk.
They're the ones who were rooted in their community,
clear in their message, willing to go everywhere

You've got a situation now where the democratic race

You struggled with black voters as a presidential candidate,

in South Carolina in 2020.
If you run again, do you feel better equipped

as mayor of South Bend, for example,
was very different from the outcome

That's fair.

Let's start there

Because as you know as a frequent guest on Fox, this is a theme. That's

Presidencies tend historically to be defined by very few issues.

What would be your emphasis?

Why?
Because of gerrymandering.
So there's a direct connection between people struggling to put food on the table and these

I believe that a great democratic movement and perhaps a future democratic president,

invested $200 million in the Texas race alone,

His great concern among Democrats,

fact that people think twice about saying what they believe because they are worried about what will

the new deal, in terms of how so many things

have been the norm for our entire lives

We could be and should be building a government

for Congress one time to when I decided to seek the presidency in 2020's race, every
time it's based on a process where I look at two things and line them up next to each
other.
One is what the moment calls for, what the office calls for, whether that office is mayor

And the other thing I look at is what do I bring to the table?
And what do I bring to the table that's different from the others?
Knowing that there are a lot of other people who would compete.
And following that process, several times led me to run through something, including,

about what your family will go through

Yeah, to put it mildly.
And, but look, there are some things,

that we should all be able to agree are not normal
to be the price of public service.
